question: Which Georgia agency licenses and regulates real estate appraisers, and how does it relate to the Georgia Real Estate Commission (GREC)?
choice_a: GREC itself licenses appraisers under the same broker/salesperson licensing chapter (Title 43, Chapter 40)
choice_b: The Georgia Real Estate Appraisers Board, established under O.C.G.A. Title 43, Chapter 39A -- a SEPARATE licensing board from GREC, not a division of it
choice_c: Appraisers in Georgia are licensed directly by the federal Appraisal Subcommittee, with no state-level board
choice_d: The Georgia Real Estate Appraisers Board is simply a subcommittee of GREC whose members are also GREC commissioners
explanation: Georgia real estate appraisers are licensed and regulated by the Georgia Real Estate Appraisers Board under O.C.G.A. Title 43, Chapter 39A -- a distinct board from the Georgia Real Estate Commission (which licenses brokers, salespersons, and CAMs under Chapter 40). A real estate license does not authorize a person to perform licensed/certified appraisals, and vice versa.
source_note: O.C.G.A. Title 43, Chapter 39A

question: How is the Georgia Real Estate Appraisers Board composed, per O.C.G.A. § 43-39A-3?
choice_a: Nine members, all licensed appraisers, elected by the appraiser community
choice_b: Three members, all gubernatorial appointees with no experience requirement
choice_c: Five members: four licensed real estate appraisers with at least three years of active appraisal experience, plus one public member with no financial affiliation with the appraisal, brokerage, or lending industries
choice_d: Seven members, a majority of whom must also hold an active real estate broker's license
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-39A-3 sets the board at five members: four licensed real estate appraisers (minimum three years' active experience) and one public member unaffiliated with the appraisal, brokerage, or lending industries -- appointed by the Governor with Senate confirmation to staggered five-year terms.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-39A-19, may a term or title denoting a Georgia appraiser license classification (e.g., "Certified Residential Appraiser") be used to refer to a firm, partnership, or corporation?
choice_a: Yes, without restriction, as long as at least one employee of the firm holds that classification
choice_b: Yes, but only for corporations, not partnerships or sole proprietorships
choice_c: The statute is silent on this point and firms may use any classification title they choose
choice_d: No -- such classification titles may only be used to refer to individuals, never to a firm, partnership, or corporation
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-39A-19 provides that an appraiser-classification title may be used to refer only to individuals -- a firm, partnership, or corporation may not hold itself out under a personal appraiser classification, since the classification attaches to the licensed individual, not the business entity.

question: If a Georgia appraiser's classification does not qualify them to perform appraisals for federally related transactions, what must their appraisal report disclose, per O.C.G.A. § 43-39A-19?
choice_a: That the report may not be used for, or may be ineligible for use in, a federally related transaction
choice_b: Nothing -- no disclosure is required regardless of the appraiser's classification
choice_c: Only the appraiser's personal contact information, with no statement about federal eligibility
choice_d: That the report is void and legally unusable for any purpose whatsoever
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-39A-19 requires an appraiser whose classification does not qualify for federally related transactions to disclose in the report that it may not be eligible for use in such a transaction -- the report can still be valid for other, non-federally-related purposes.

question: As a matter of general national appraiser-licensing structure (which Georgia's appraiser classifications follow), how does a "Certified Residential" appraiser classification typically differ from a "Certified General" classification?
choice_a: Certified Residential is authorized for complex commercial appraisal assignments of any value, while Certified General is limited to single-family homes
choice_b: Certified Residential authorizes appraisal of 1-4 unit residential properties (regardless of transaction complexity or value); Certified General authorizes appraisal of all property types, including complex commercial and residential property, with no similar dollar/complexity ceiling
choice_c: The two classifications are identical in scope and differ only in name
choice_d: Certified Residential is a purely honorary designation carrying no additional appraisal authority beyond a Trainee license
explanation: Consistent with the national Appraiser Qualifications Board classification structure that Georgia's board administers, a Certified Residential credential authorizes appraisal of one-to-four unit residential property without a complexity/value ceiling, while a Certified General credential additionally authorizes appraisal of all other property types, including commercial and complex assignments.
source_note: hedge: standard national Appraiser Qualifications Board (AQB) classification structure

question: What is a "Trainee" (or "Registered Trainee") appraiser classification, under the national licensing structure Georgia's appraiser board administers?
choice_a: The highest appraiser classification, reserved for appraisers with 20+ years of experience
choice_b: A classification that permits fully independent commercial appraisal work with no supervision
choice_c: An entry-level classification permitting an individual to perform appraisal work only under the direct supervision of a properly credentialed supervising appraiser, as a path toward an independent license classification
choice_d: A designation used only for appraisers who exclusively review other appraisers' completed reports
explanation: A Trainee appraiser classification is an entry-level credential that allows the trainee to perform appraisal work only under a supervising appraiser's direct oversight, while accumulating the experience hours required to qualify for an independent (Licensed or Certified) classification.
source_note: hedge: standard national Appraiser Qualifications Board (AQB) classification structure

question: What is the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP)?
choice_a: A single federal law that directly regulates only VA-guaranteed loan appraisals
choice_b: A voluntary marketing brochure published by the National Association of Realtors with no binding effect on appraisers
choice_c: A standard used only outside the United States and not applicable to Georgia-licensed appraisers
choice_d: The generally recognized ethical and performance standards for the appraisal profession in the United States, developed by the Appraisal Standards Board and adopted/enforced by state appraiser regulatory boards (including Georgia's) as a condition of licensure
explanation: USPAP sets the recognized ethical and performance standards for the U.S. appraisal profession, developed by the Appraisal Foundation's Appraisal Standards Board. State appraiser boards, including Georgia's, require licensed and certified appraisers to comply with USPAP as a condition of licensure and in performing appraisal assignments.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-regulatory framework

question: What does USPAP's "Ethics Rule" generally require regarding appraiser independence and advocacy?
choice_a: That an appraiser must perform assignments with impartiality, objectivity, and independence, and without accommodating personal interests -- prohibiting an appraiser from developing or reporting a predetermined, biased, or advocacy-driven opinion of value
choice_b: That an appraiser may adjust the reported value upward if requested by the lender who ordered the report, so long as the client agrees
choice_c: That an appraiser must always render a value at least equal to the contract sale price
choice_d: That an appraiser must act as an advocate for whichever party is paying the appraisal fee
explanation: USPAP's Ethics Rule requires appraisers to act with impartiality, objectivity, and independence, without personal bias or advocacy for any party to the assignment -- an appraiser may not agree in advance to report a predetermined value or a value favorable to any party's interests.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-regulatory framework (USPAP)

question: What is the general purpose of the federal Appraiser Independence Requirements (AIR), which apply to consumer credit transactions secured by a consumer's principal dwelling?
choice_a: To require the seller, rather than the lender, to select and directly pay the appraiser
choice_b: To prohibit lenders, loan production staff, and other interested parties from improperly influencing an appraiser's independent judgment, such as by pressuring for a predetermined value or selecting appraisers based on their willingness to inflate valuations
choice_c: To prohibit any communication whatsoever between a loan officer and an appraiser, even for administrative scheduling purposes
choice_d: To eliminate the need for any home appraisal on loans below $1,000,000
explanation: The federal Appraiser Independence Requirements are designed to prevent lenders, mortgage brokers, and other interested parties from coercing or improperly influencing an appraiser's independent value opinion -- a response to appraisal-inflation practices identified as contributing to the 2008 financial crisis.
source_note: hedge: standard federal law (Dodd-Frank Act / Regulation Z appraiser independence provisions)

question: How does "market value" -- the value opinion sought in most mortgage-lending appraisals -- generally differ from "market price" (the price a property actually sold for)?
choice_a: Market value and market price are legally identical terms with no meaningful distinction
choice_b: Market price only applies to commercial property, while market value applies only to residential property
choice_c: Market value is a theoretical, probable price under specified conditions (e.g., a willing, typically motivated buyer and seller, reasonable market exposure, arm's-length dealing, no undue duress); market price is simply the actual, historical transaction price of a specific sale, which may or may not reflect those conditions
choice_d: Market value is always lower than market price by a fixed statutory percentage
explanation: Market value is a defined, theoretical estimate of the most probable price under normal, arm's-length market conditions; market price is simply what a property actually sold for in a specific transaction, which can be influenced by atypical motivation, financing, or duress that market value assumes away.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What is the difference between an appraisal's "effective date of value" and the date the appraisal report is signed/delivered?
choice_a: The two dates must always be identical under USPAP
choice_b: The effective date of value refers only to when the appraiser was licensed, not to any specific property valuation date
choice_c: The report date always precedes the effective date of value
choice_d: The effective date of value is the date to which the value opinion applies (often, but not always, the date of the appraiser's inspection); the report date is when the appraiser completes and signs the written report, which may be later than the effective date
explanation: The effective date of value is the specific date to which the appraiser's value conclusion applies (commonly the inspection date for a current-value appraisal, but it can be a past or future date for retrospective or prospective appraisals). The report date -- when the appraiser signs and delivers the report -- is often later than the effective date.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content (USPAP)

question: What does the appraisal/land-economics principle of "assemblage" refer to, and what related concept describes the resulting value change?
choice_a: Assemblage is the combining of two or more separately owned parcels under single ownership/control; "plottage value" describes the resulting increase in value (if any) that the combined, larger parcel achieves above the sum of the individual parcels' separate values
choice_b: Assemblage refers only to assembling building materials on a construction site, unrelated to land value
choice_c: Assemblage always decreases the combined value of the parcels involved
choice_d: Plottage value refers to the value of a single, non-combined parcel with no relationship to assemblage
explanation: Assemblage is the act of combining two or more adjoining parcels into one ownership; when the resulting larger, combined parcel is worth more than the sum of the individual parcels' values (e.g., because it now supports a more valuable use), that increment is called plottage value.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: In the cost approach, how does a property's "effective age" generally differ from its "actual (chronological) age"?
choice_a: The two terms are always numerically identical for every property
choice_b: Actual (chronological) age is the number of years since the structure was actually built; effective age is the age indicated by the property's condition, utility, and remaining economic life relative to comparable properties -- a well-maintained or updated older building may have an effective age lower than its actual age
choice_c: Actual age is the age indicated by the condition and utility of the improvements as perceived in the market; effective age is simply the number of years since construction
choice_d: Effective age applies only to vacant land, never to improved property
explanation: Actual (chronological) age is the true number of years since the structure was built. Effective age reflects the building's condition and remaining utility as perceived by the market -- a 40-year-old home that has been extensively renovated may have an effective age well below 40 years, while a poorly maintained newer home could have a higher effective age than its actual age.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What does the appraisal principle of "increasing and decreasing returns" (also called diminishing returns) describe?
choice_a: That every additional dollar spent on improving a property always adds at least one dollar of value, without limit
choice_b: That land value only increases and never decreases over any period of time
choice_c: That improvements to land and structures increase value up to a point of maximum return; beyond that point, additional expenditures add progressively less value than they cost, and may eventually add no value or even detract from it
choice_d: That the principle applies exclusively to agricultural land, never to residential or commercial property
explanation: The principle of increasing and decreasing (diminishing) returns holds that additional improvements add value up to an optimal point; beyond that point, each additional dollar spent yields progressively smaller value increases, and over-improvement can eventually add less value than its cost.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What does the appraisal principle of "supply and demand" hold with respect to real property value?
choice_a: Real property value is set exclusively by construction cost and is unaffected by market supply or demand
choice_b: Demand for real property is always constant and never fluctuates over time
choice_c: Supply and demand affects only vacant land, never improved property
choice_d: Value tends to rise as supply decreases relative to demand, or as demand increases relative to supply, and to fall under the opposite conditions -- the same basic economic relationship as with other goods, though real estate's supply typically adjusts more slowly due to the time required to develop new property
explanation: Like other economic goods, real property value responds to the relative balance of supply and demand -- but real estate supply is comparatively slow to adjust to changing demand, since new construction, zoning approval, and development take substantial time, often producing more pronounced short-term price swings than in markets with faster-adjusting supply.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What is a key structural difference between the reproduction cost and the replacement cost concepts used in the cost approach to value?
choice_a: Reproduction cost estimates the cost to construct an exact replica of the subject improvements, using the same materials, design, and construction standards (including any obsolete features); replacement cost estimates the cost to construct a building of equivalent utility using current materials, design, and construction standards -- which sidesteps the need to separately measure functional obsolescence caused by outdated design
choice_b: The two terms are perfectly interchangeable with no conceptual distinction
choice_c: Reproduction cost applies only to land, while replacement cost applies only to improvements
choice_d: Replacement cost is always higher than reproduction cost for any property
explanation: Reproduction cost estimates building an exact duplicate (same materials/design, obsolete features included), requiring the appraiser to separately deduct for functional obsolescence. Replacement cost estimates a modern-equivalent-utility structure using current standards, which inherently avoids reproducing outdated/obsolete design features.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What three general methods do appraisers commonly use to estimate depreciation under the cost approach?
choice_a: Only the income capitalization method applies to estimating depreciation
choice_b: The age-life (economic age-life) method, the market extraction (sales comparison) method, and the breakdown (cost-to-cure/observed condition) method
choice_c: Depreciation can only be estimated by directly asking the property owner for their opinion
choice_d: Depreciation is always assumed to be zero for any property under ten years old
explanation: Common depreciation-estimation methods include the age-life method (ratio of effective age to total economic life), the market extraction method (deriving depreciation from paired sales of comparable properties), and the breakdown (or observed condition/cost-to-cure) method, which itemizes each specific cause of depreciation separately.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: In the sales comparison approach, when a comparable property is superior to the subject property in some feature, how is the dollar adjustment applied?
choice_a: The adjustment is added to the comparable's sale price, since the subject would need to be worth more to match the superior comparable
choice_b: The adjustment is always applied to the subject property's assessed tax value instead of the comparable's sale price
choice_c: The adjustment is subtracted from the comparable's sale price, because the comparable's advantage over the subject must be removed to make it a fair proxy for the (inferior) subject
choice_d: No adjustment is ever made for superior features; only inferior features are adjusted
explanation: In the sales comparison approach, adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's. If a comparable is superior to the subject in some feature, its price is adjusted DOWNWARD (subtracted) to remove the value of that advantage, since the subject lacks it. Conversely, if a comparable is inferior, its price is adjusted upward.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What is a "restricted (or restricted-use)" appraisal report, as compared to a more detailed appraisal report format?
choice_a: A report format that omits the appraiser's signature and is therefore not a valid appraisal
choice_b: A report format used exclusively for appraisals of government-owned property
choice_c: A report format that legally cannot be relied upon by any party, including the client
choice_d: A concise report format intended for use only by the client, containing a brief summary of the appraiser's analysis and conclusions rather than the fuller explanation found in more detailed report formats -- appropriate only where the client understands the limited detail is sufficient for their intended use
explanation: A restricted-use appraisal report presents a brief summary of the appraiser's analysis and value conclusion, intended for use by the client alone and understood to contain limited detail -- less appropriate where multiple, less-informed users may rely on the report.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content (USPAP report-type framework)

question: What is the purpose of an "appraisal review," as distinct from performing a new original appraisal?
choice_a: An appraisal review is the process of examining another appraiser's report to form an opinion about the quality, adequacy, and credibility of that report's analysis and conclusions -- not necessarily to develop an independent opinion of the property's value
choice_b: An appraisal review is simply a second, independent original appraisal performed without reference to the first
choice_c: An appraisal review may only be performed by the original appraiser who wrote the report
choice_d: An appraisal review is a purely administrative filing step with no substantive analysis involved
explanation: An appraisal review evaluates the quality, completeness, and credibility of another appraiser's report and its conclusions -- the reviewer may (but is not required to) also develop their own independent opinion of value, depending on the scope of the review assignment.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content (USPAP review framework)

question: How does a "desktop" appraisal generally differ from a traditional appraisal that includes a physical property inspection?
choice_a: A desktop appraisal is legally identical to a full inspection appraisal in every respect
choice_b: A desktop appraisal is developed using data sources such as public records, MLS data, and other third-party information, without the appraiser personally inspecting the property in person -- increasingly used for certain lower-risk loan transactions under applicable lending guidelines
choice_c: A desktop appraisal requires two separate in-person inspections instead of one
choice_d: A desktop appraisal can only be performed on vacant land, never on improved property
explanation: A desktop appraisal relies on existing data (public records, prior listing/MLS photos, tax records, aerial imagery, etc.) rather than a personal on-site inspection by the appraiser -- used in some lending contexts for eligible, typically lower-risk transactions under applicable investor/agency guidelines.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: Why is the sales comparison approach generally considered less reliable for a highly unique, special-purpose property (such as a church, school, or specialized manufacturing facility) than for a typical single-family home?
choice_a: Because special-purpose properties are always worth exactly their original construction cost with no exceptions
choice_b: Because the sales comparison approach cannot legally be applied to any commercial property under any circumstances
choice_c: Because there are typically too few (or no) comparable sales of similarly unique properties to support a reliable adjustment grid, making the cost approach (or, if income-producing, the income approach) generally more reliable for such properties
choice_d: Because special-purpose properties never sell and therefore have no market value at all
explanation: The sales comparison approach depends on a sufficient pool of genuinely comparable recent sales; special-purpose properties (churches, schools, factories built for a specific use) often lack enough comparable sales for a reliable analysis, making the cost approach (or income approach, for income-producing special-purpose property) typically more reliable.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: What does the appraisal principle of "balance" hold with respect to the four agents of production (land, labor, capital, and management/entrepreneurial coordination)?
choice_a: Balance requires that all four agents of production always be allocated in exactly equal proportions on every property
choice_b: Balance refers exclusively to a lender's debt-to-income underwriting calculation, not to appraisal theory
choice_c: The principle of balance applies only to raw land with no improvements
choice_d: Value tends to be maximized when the various agents of production (and the mix of land use / improvement types within a neighborhood) exist in appropriate proportion to one another -- an imbalance in either direction can reduce value
explanation: The principle of balance holds that value tends to be maximized when the agents of production, and the overall mix of land uses/improvements, are proportionate -- an over- or under-allocation among land, labor, capital, and management (or an imbalanced mix of uses within an area) tends to reduce overall value.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content

question: In a real estate purchase contract with a financing contingency, what is commonly referred to as an 'appraisal gap,' and how is it often addressed?
choice_a: The situation where the appraised value comes in below the agreed contract price, creating a shortfall the buyer must cover with additional cash, renegotiate, or address through a contract provision (such as an appraisal-gap coverage clause) if the transaction is to proceed at the original price
choice_b: A gap in time between when the appraisal is ordered and when it is completed, with no bearing on price or financing
choice_c: The difference between the property's assessed tax value and its insured replacement cost
choice_d: A term describing a vacant lot with no improvements
explanation: An 'appraisal gap' describes the shortfall when a lender's appraisal comes in below the agreed contract price -- since most lenders will only finance based on the lower of appraised value or purchase price -- requiring the buyer to cover the gap with additional cash, renegotiate the price, or rely on a contract provision addressing how such a gap will be handled if the parties want the deal to proceed at the original price.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal/financing-practice content

question: A comparable property sold for $345,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $12,000 for a fourth bedroom the comparable has but the subject lacks; add $8,000 for an updated kitchen the subject has but the comparable lacks; subtract $5,000 for a larger lot the comparable has. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$12,000 (a fourth bedroom the comparable has but the subject lacks), +$8,000 (an updated kitchen the subject has but the comparable lacks), -$5,000 (a larger lot the comparable has) = $-9,000. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $345,000 - $9,000 = $336,000. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content; arithmetic independently verified

question: A comparable property sold for $412,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $9,500 for a two-car garage the comparable has but the subject lacks; add $15,000 for a finished basement the subject has but the comparable lacks. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$9,500 (a two-car garage the comparable has but the subject lacks), +$15,000 (a finished basement the subject has but the comparable lacks) = +$5,500. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $412,000 + $5,500 = $417,500. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: A comparable property sold for $289,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $18,000 for a pool the comparable has but the subject lacks; add $6,000 for superior condition of the subject versus the comparable; add $7,000 for one fewer bathroom in the comparable. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$18,000 (a pool the comparable has but the subject lacks), +$6,000 (superior condition of the subject versus the comparable), +$7,000 (one fewer bathroom in the comparable) = $-5,000. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $289,000 - $5,000 = $284,000. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: A comparable property sold for $520,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $22,000 for a larger square footage in the comparable (250 sq ft more); add $10,000 for a better view from the subject. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$22,000 (a larger square footage in the comparable (250 sq ft more)), +$10,000 (a better view from the subject) = $-12,000. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $520,000 - $12,000 = $508,000. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: A comparable property sold for $176,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: add $9,000 for an inferior location for the comparable versus the subject; subtract $4,000 for a newer roof on the comparable. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = +$9,000 (an inferior location for the comparable versus the subject), -$4,000 (a newer roof on the comparable) = +$5,000. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $176,000 + $5,000 = $181,000. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: A comparable property sold for $398,500. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $11,000 for a detached garage the comparable has but the subject lacks; add $6,500 for a screened porch the subject has but the comparable lacks; subtract $3,000 for superior landscaping at the comparable. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$11,000 (a detached garage the comparable has but the subject lacks), +$6,500 (a screened porch the subject has but the comparable lacks), -$3,000 (superior landscaping at the comparable) = $-7,500. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $398,500 - $7,500 = $391,000. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: A comparable property sold for $455,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $14,000 for a renovated primary bathroom at the comparable that the subject lacks; add $5,000 for a corner lot premium for the subject. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$14,000 (a renovated primary bathroom at the comparable that the subject lacks), +$5,000 (a corner lot premium for the subject) = $-9,000. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $455,000 - $9,000 = $446,000. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: A comparable property sold for $263,000. An appraiser makes the following dollar adjustments to the comparable when analyzing it against the subject property: subtract $6,000 for one additional half-bath at the comparable; add $4,500 for a larger deck at the subject; subtract $8,000 for superior school zone for the comparable. What is the resulting adjusted (indicated) value from this comparable?
explanation: Net adjustment = -$6,000 (one additional half-bath at the comparable), +$4,500 (a larger deck at the subject), -$8,000 (superior school zone for the comparable) = $-9,500. Adjusted value = comparable's sale price + net adjustment = $263,000 - $9,500 = $253,500. Remember: adjustments are always made to the COMPARABLE's price, never to the subject's.

question: An appraiser estimates the current reproduction cost of a building's improvements at $310,000. The building has an effective age of 8 years and a total economic life of 60 years. Land value is separately estimated at $95,000. Using the age-life method to estimate accrued depreciation, what is the property's total indicated value under the cost approach?
explanation: Accrued depreciation = (effective age / economic life) x reproduction cost = (8/60) x $310,000 = $41,333. Depreciated improvement value = $310,000 - $41,333 = $268,667. Adding land value: $268,667 + $95,000 = $363,667.
source_note: hedge: standard national appraisal-theory content (cost approach, age-life depreciation method); arithmetic independently verified

question: An appraiser estimates the current reproduction cost of a building's improvements at $420,000. The building has an effective age of 12 years and a total economic life of 55 years. Land value is separately estimated at $140,000. Using the age-life method to estimate accrued depreciation, what is the property's total indicated value under the cost approach?
explanation: Accrued depreciation = (effective age / economic life) x reproduction cost = (12/55) x $420,000 = $91,636. Depreciated improvement value = $420,000 - $91,636 = $328,364. Adding land value: $328,364 + $140,000 = $468,364.

question: An appraiser estimates the current reproduction cost of a building's improvements at $265,000. The building has an effective age of 15 years and a total economic life of 50 years. Land value is separately estimated at $82,000. Using the age-life method to estimate accrued depreciation, what is the property's total indicated value under the cost approach?
explanation: Accrued depreciation = (effective age / economic life) x reproduction cost = (15/50) x $265,000 = $79,500. Depreciated improvement value = $265,000 - $79,500 = $185,500. Adding land value: $185,500 + $82,000 = $267,500.

question: An appraiser estimates the current reproduction cost of a building's improvements at $510,000. The building has an effective age of 6 years and a total economic life of 65 years. Land value is separately estimated at $175,000. Using the age-life method to estimate accrued depreciation, what is the property's total indicated value under the cost approach?
explanation: Accrued depreciation = (effective age / economic life) x reproduction cost = (6/65) x $510,000 = $47,077. Depreciated improvement value = $510,000 - $47,077 = $462,923. Adding land value: $462,923 + $175,000 = $637,923.

question: An appraiser estimates the current reproduction cost of a building's improvements at $198,000. The building has an effective age of 20 years and a total economic life of 45 years. Land value is separately estimated at $68,000. Using the age-life method to estimate accrued depreciation, what is the property's total indicated value under the cost approach?
explanation: Accrued depreciation = (effective age / economic life) x reproduction cost = (20/45) x $198,000 = $88,000. Depreciated improvement value = $198,000 - $88,000 = $110,000. Adding land value: $110,000 + $68,000 = $178,000.
